./data/fulltext_screening_context_2026-07-09_llm_data_input_fullsections_smoke/fulltext_screening_input.json:56:    "full_text_context": "[data_source: Large-Scale, Multi-Modal Dataset for Computational Pathology]
We created PRISM-12M, a large-scale dataset comprising over 12 million spatially co-registered pairs of image patches linking H&E histology with corresponding single-cell-resolution spatial omics data (Fig. 1a). This curated dataset was generated using a custom processing pipeline that performs image quality control, co-registration, and the extraction of paired patches from wholeslide images. This process ensures direct spatial correspondence between high-quality tissue morphology and molecular data (Extended Data Fig. 1).

PRISM-12M includes fourteen different tissue types, representing both normal and pathological tissues from humans and mice (Fig. 1b). This variety of tissue types and conditions ensures that computational models developed using this dataset are generalizable across various biological and pathological contexts. Currently, PRISM-12M includes two single-cell-resolution spatial omics modalities: spatial proteomics data generated using Cyclic Immunofluorescence (CyCIF) and CO-DEtection by indeXing (CODEX) platforms, which collectively cover 166 unique proteins. Additionally, it includes spatial transcriptomics data generated using the Xenium platform, featuring 1,261 RNA species (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 2). The multi-modal nature of PRISM-12M enables the creation of unified computational frameworks that can predict protein and RNA spatial expression patterns from H&E images alone. The scale and diversity of PRISM-12M make it an invaluable resource for developing and evaluating computational methods that link tissue morphology to molecular phenotypes, addressing a critical challenge in computational pathology.

We formulated the multi-modal learning task as a conditional image generation problem with natural language conditioning. For predicting protein and RNA expression, we used structured text prompts formatted as: "predict [protein/gene name] protein/RNA expression", which explicitly specifies the target molecular modality and identity. For the DAPI-to-H&E translation task, we used the prompt "predict corresponding H&E image", framing the nuclear stain as input for predicting the histological appearance. These prompts enable flexible task conditioning within a unified framework and can be adapted to additional modalities or prediction targets.",

content=""cessibility data. The workflow begins with data preprocessing using single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (scATAC)-pro or Cell Ranger ATAC, followed by peak calling with MACS2 and differential accessibility analysis to detect open chromatin regions and perform differential accessibility analysis to highlight regulatory differences among cell populations. Transcription factor activity is then inferred using chromVAR, incorporating motif enrichment and footprinting analysis. Finally, SCENIC+ is applied to reconstruct transcriptional regulatory networks, enabling in-depth exploration of epigenetic mechanisms at the single-cell level. This integrative approach offers a robust framework for decoding the regulatory landscape and understanding cellular heterogeneity in complex biological systems...."" /><meta property=""og:image"" content=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/SocialThumb.02118581-202603000-00013.F1.jpeg"" /><meta property=""og:image:width"" content=""2400"" /><meta property=""og:image:height"" content=""1482"" /><meta property=""og:url"" content=""https://journals.lww.com/bls/fulltext/2026/03000/a_pipeline_for_single_cell_chromatin_accessibility.13.aspx"" /><meta property=""twitter:card"" content=""summary"" /><meta name=""robots"" content=""index, follow, noarchive"" /><meta name=""WT.sv"" content=""WEB01"" /><meta name=""Title"" content=""Blood Science"" /><style id=""SPThemeHideForms"" type=""text/css"">body {opacity:0 !important}</style>

    function alerts_SaveSubscriptionTypeInHiddenField(url, subscriptionType, journalId, yearId, issueId, articleId) {
        if (journalId && yearId && issueId && articleId) {
            logCounterDataAlertWhenCitedSynchronously(journalId, yearId, issueId, articleId);
        }
        
        $('#' + 'ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscriptionType').val(subscriptionType);
        $('#' + 'ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenJournalId').val(journalId);
        if (url)
            window.location = url;
        else 
            __doPostBack('hypSubscribeToAlerts');
        return false;
    }

    function alerts_ShowSubscribeeTOCPopup(journalTitle, journalId, subscriptionType, displaySubscriptionType) {
        $('#' + 'ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscriptionType').val(subscriptionType);
        var subscribeToEtocPopup = $find('subscribeToEtoc');
        subscribeToEtocPopup.show();
        document.getElementsByTagName( 'html' )[0].classList.add('no-scroll');
        var modelPopupState = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscribeToEtocPopupState');
        var emailTextBox = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_txtEmailAddress');
        var thanksPanel = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_pnlAuthenticatedUser');
        var mainPanel = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_pnlMain');
        var thankYouMessageUnAuthenticated = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_lblThankYouMessage');
        var thankYouMessageAuthenticated = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_lblAuthenticatedUserTitle');

        if (!displaySubscriptionType) {
            displaySubscriptionType = subscriptionType;
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showthanksmessage') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = ""block"";
            mainPanel.style.display = ""none"";
            thankYouMessageAuthenticated.innerHTML = ""Thank you for subscribing to the "" + displaySubscriptionType + "" for "" + journalTitle + ""."";
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = ""none"";
            mainPanel.style.display = ""block"";

            thankYouMessageUnAuthenticated.innerHTML = ""Thank you for choosing to subscribe to the "" + displaySubscriptionType + "" for "" + journalTitle + ""."";
        }

        if ($('.etoc-popup') != null) {
            document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenJournalId').value = journalId;

            if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail')
                emailTextBox.focus();
        }
    }

    $('.js-close').on('click', function () {
        document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_txtEmailAddress').value = """";
        document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_cvEmailError').style.display = ""none"";
        var pageUrl = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenConfirmSubscriptionPageUrl');
        var subscribeeTocPopup = $find('subscribeToEtoc');
        if (subscribeeTocPopup != null) {
            subscribeeTocPopup.hide();
            document.getElementsByTagName( 'html' )[0].classList.remove('no-scroll');
            if (pageUrl.value !== '' && pageUrl.value !== window.location.pathname)
                window.location = pageUrl.value;
        }
        return false;
    });
</script>

    </ul></section><section class=""ejp-article-tabs"" id=""abstractWrap""><div class=""ejp-article-tabs__tablist"" role=""tablist"" aria-label=""Tabs""><button class=""ejp-article-tabs__tablist-item"" role=""tab"" aria-selected=""false"" aria-controls=""panel1"" id=""tab1"" tabIndex=""0"">Abstract</button><button class=""ejp-article-tabs__tablist-item ejp-article-tabs__ai-summary"" role=""tab"" aria-selected=""false"" aria-controls=""panel4"" id=""tab4"" tabIndex=""0"" onclick=""LogArticleSubTabClickEventToCounterData('AISummary')"">Plain Language Summary</button><hr class=""ejp-article-tabs__tablist-slider"" style=""left: 0;"">

    <div class=""ejp-article-tabs__tabpanel"" id=""panel1"" role=""tabpanel"" aria-labelledby=""tab1"">
      <div id=""article-abstract-content1"">
        <div class=""ejp-article-text-abstract"">
          <p>Single-cell chromatin accessibility analysis enables high-resolution dissection of regulatory elements and gene regulatory mechanisms. However, standardized and comprehensive analysis workflows remain limited. In this study, we present a streamlined pipeline for analyzing single-cell chromatin accessibility data. The workflow begins with data preprocessing using single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (scATAC)-pro or Cell Ranger ATAC, followed by peak calling with MACS2 and differential accessibility analysis to detect open chromatin regions and perform differential accessibility analysis to highlight regulatory differences among cell populations. Transcription factor activity is then inferred using chromVAR, incorporating motif enrichment and footprinting analysis. Finally, SCENIC+ is applied to reconstruct transcriptional regulatory networks, enabling in-depth exploration of epigenetic mechanisms at the single-cell level. This integrative approach offers a robust framework for decoding the regulatory landscape and understanding cellular heterogeneity in complex biological systems.</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class=""ejp-article-tabs__tabpanel"" id=""panel4"" role=""tabpanel"" aria-labelledby=""tab4"">
      <div id=""article-abstract-content3"">
        <p><span class=""ejp-indicator"">Plain Language Summary</span>This study introduces a streamlined pipeline for analyzing single-cell chromatin accessibility data, which helps uncover regulatory elements and gene mechanisms. The process starts with data preprocessing using scATAC-pro or Cell Ranger ATAC, followed by peak calling with MACS2 to identify open chromatin regions. Differential accessibility analysis highlights regulatory differences among cell populations. Transcription factor activity is inferred using chromVAR, which includes motif enrichment and footprinting analysis. SCENIC+ is then used to reconstruct transcriptional regulatory networks. This comprehensive workflow provides a robust framework for exploring epigenetic mechanisms and cellular diversity in complex biological systems.</p>

    </div></section><div class=""ejp-fulltext-content js-ejp-fulltext-content""><section id=""ArticleBody""><h2 class=""ejp-article-outline-heading"" data-level=""1"" id=""JCL0"">1. INTRODUCTION</h2>
      <p id=""JCL-P-3"">Various approaches have been developed to study chromatin accessibility, such as deoxyribonuclease I hypersensitivity sequencing (DNase-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R1 R2 R3"">1–3</a></sup></sup> formaldehyde-assisted isolation of regulatory elements (FAIRE-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R4"">4</a></sup></sup> micrococcal nuclease digestion with sequencing (MNase-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R5"">5</a></sup></sup><sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">,</sup><sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R6"">6</a></sup></sup> assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing (ATAC-seq),<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R7"">7</a></sup></sup> and nucleosome occupancy and methylome sequencing (NOMe-seq).<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R8"">8</a></sup></sup> ATAC-seq is a method for mapping chromatin accessibility genome-wide using a hyperactive Tn5 transposase, which inserts sequencing adapters into accessible chromatin regions.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R9"">9</a></sup></sup> ATAC-seq is faster, simpler, and requires fewer cells than DNase-seq and MNase-seq, which are more time-consuming and costly due to their large cell requirements and separate assays.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R7"">7</a></sup></sup> However, bulk ATAC-seq is unable to determine chromatin accessibility at the single-cell level, thereby limiting its application in identifying cell subpopulations. To address these limitations, single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq) has been developed. Leveraging the advantages of the ATAC-seq protocol, scATAC-seq can measure chromatin accessibility on the single-cell level and the data richness of single-cell genomics has been substantially expanded.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R10"">10</a></sup></sup> scATAC-seq data has become a popular tool for examining chromatin accessibility at the single-cell level. scATAC-seq has emerged as a powerful approach for dissecting cell type-specific regulatory programs, identifying rare cell populations, and inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs).</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-4"">However, scATAC-seq data analysis poses unique computational challenges, necessitating robust pipelines for preprocessing, peak calling, differential accessibility analysis, motif enrichment, and regulatory network reconstruction.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-5"">Current pipelines for scATAC-seq analysis offer a diverse toolkit, each with unique strengths and limitations. ArchR stands out for its scalability and rich visualization features, making it ideal for large datasets, though it can be memory-intensive and primarily R-based.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R11"">11</a></sup></sup> Signac,<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R12"">12</a></sup></sup> as part of the Seurat ecosystem, excels at multi-omic integration with scRNA-seq and offers flexibility, but may struggle with very large datasets and lacks some automation. SnapATAC<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R13"">13</a></sup></sup> is highly efficient and fast, particularly well-suited for large-scale clustering, yet its bin-based approach can lead to lower resolution at the peak level. cisTopic<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R14"">14</a></sup></sup> provides interpretable topic modeling for regulatory programs but may have limitations in scalability and integration with other data types. MAESTRO<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R15"">15</a></sup></sup> is valuable for joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq analysis, but can be complex to configure. Meanwhile, Cell Ranger ATAC is user-friendly and standardized for 10x data, but lacks flexibility for non-10x platforms or advanced customization. scATAC-pro<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R16"">16</a></sup></sup> is a comprehensive tool for processing, analyzing, and visualizing single-cell chromatin accessibility sequencing data. Overall, tool choice depends on specific goals such as integration, scale, or user expertise, and no single pipeline yet dominates across all criteria. The current protocol provides a pipeline for downstream bioinformatics analysis of scATAC-seq (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F1', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 1</a></strong>).</p><section class=""ejp-r-article-images""><figure class=""ejp-r-article-images__figure""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__image-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F1', '02118581-202603000-00013')""><img class=""ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load"" src=""javascript:void(0);"" data-src=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F1.jpeg"" data-srcset=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F1.jpeg 2x"" srcset="""" alt=""F1""></a><figcaption class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F1', '02118581-202603000-00013')"">Figure 1.: </a><div class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text"">Schematic workflow for single-cell ATAC-seq data processing and downstream analysis. The analysis pipeline begins with raw sequencing data (FASTQs) processed using Cell Ranger ATAC and scATAC-pro for alignment, demultiplexing, trimming, mapping, and filtering. ArchR is then used to create Arrow files and projects, followed by quality control and doublet filtering. Dimensionality reduction and clustering enable identification of cell populations. Downstream analyses include peak calling, identification of marker peaks and features, TF motif search, and TF footprint analysis. ATAC = assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, TF = transcription factor.</div></figcaption></figure></section><h2 class=""ejp-article-outline-heading"" data-level=""1"" id=""JCL1"">2. PREPARATION</h2>
      <p id=""JCL-P-6"">For data analysis, it is essential to have access to a computational server or a high-performance computing environment, since handling data at this scale can be too demanding for most regular computers. A fundamental understanding of command-line tools and bioinformatics is required for implementing the pipeline.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-7"">Hardware requirements:</p>
      <ul id=""JCL1-4"" class=""wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet"">
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">High-performance computing server (minimum 64 GB RAM recommended).</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">Linux-based system (Ubuntu 20.04 or CentOS preferred).</li>
      </ul>
      <p id=""JCL-P-10"">Data requirements:</p>
      <ul id=""JCL1-6"" class=""wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet"">
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">Single-cell ATAC-seq raw sequencing reads in FASTQ format: 5k peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a Healthy Donor (Next GEM v1.1) (5k PBMCs from a Healthy Donor [Next GEM v1.1]—10x Genomics).</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">Cryopreserved human PBMCs from a healthy female donor aged 25 were obtained by 10x Genomics from AllCells. Epi Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression dataset analyzed using Cell Ranger ARC 2.0.0 (PBMC from a Healthy Donor—Granulocytes Removed Through Cell Sorting [3k]—10x Genomics).</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">Genome reference (eg, human hg38, mouse mm10): Download the reference genome. Download the appropriate reference genome file from the 10x Genomics official website (<span><a href=""https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/downloads/latest"" onclick=""javascript:window.open('https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/downloads/latest');return false"">https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/downloads/latest</a></span>) based on the species studied. For example, download the GRCh38 reference genome for human data.</li>
      </ul>

      </div><br><h2 class=""ejp-article-outline-heading"" data-level=""1"" id=""JCL3"">4. STEP-BY-STEP METHOD DETAILS</h2>
      <p id=""JCL-P-15""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 1: Data preprocessing with Cell Ranger ATAC</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-16"">Before analysis, ensure Cell Ranger ATAC is installed, the reference genome files are downloaded, and the sequencing-derived FASTQ files are prepared.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-17"">Install Cell Ranger ATAC Refer to the official documentation(<span><a href=""https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/pipelines/latest/installation"" onclick=""javascript:window.open('https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/pipelines/latest/installation');return false"">https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-atac/software/pipelines/latest/installation</a></span>) for installation.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-18"">1.1 Create a working directory and extract data</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-19"">>mkdir scATAC_analysis</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-20"">>cd scATAC_analysis</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-21"">1.2 Run Cell Ranger ATAC to generate single-nucleus accessibility counts</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-22"">For the subsequent analysis in this tutorial, we will utilize the dataset titled <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">5k PBMCs from a Healthy Donor (Next GEM v1.1</em>) provided by 10x Genomics.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-23"">> cellranger-atac count</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-24"">--id=atac_pbmc_5k_analysis \</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-25"">--reference=/path/to/reference/refdata-cellranger-arc-GRCh38-2020-A-2.0.0/ \</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-26"">--fastqs=/path/to/fastq_files/atac_pbmc_5k_nextgem_fastqs \</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-27"">--sample= atac_pbmc_5k_nextgem \</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-28"">--localcores=8 \</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-29"">--localmem=64</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-30"">1.3 Check Output Files</p>
      <ul id=""JCL3-11"" class=""wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet"">
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">outs/summary.csv: Quality control statistics</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">outs/filtered_peak_bc_matrix.h5: Cell-by-peak matrix</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">outs/cloupe.cloupe: Visualization file for Loupe Browser</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">outs/fragments.tsv.gz: Input File Types in ArchR</li>
      </ul>
      <p id=""JCL-P-35"">Note: Cell Ranger ATAC is tightly integrated with the data format and platform of 10x Genomics single-cell ATAC-seq, making it potentially incompatible with data from other sources. Therefore, we introduce an alternative tool here: scATAC-pro.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-36""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 2: Data preprocessing with scATAC-Pro</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-37"">scATAC-pro is an integrated open-source computational toolkit designed for processing, analyzing, and visualizing sequencing datasets from single-cell chromatin accessibility experiments.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R16"">16</a></sup></sup> The scATAC-pro framework comprises 2 core functional units: a data processing unit and a downstream analysis unit. The data processing unit accepts raw FASTQ files as input and generates critical outputs, including a peak-by-cell count matrix, a quality control (QC) metrics report, and genome browser-compatible track files. This protocol focuses specifically on the data processing pipeline. Its workflow encompasses 7 key modules: sample demultiplexing, adapter sequence removal, read alignment to a reference genome, chromatin accessibility peak detection, cell barcode identification, genomic track file generation, and comprehensive quality assessment.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-38"">2.1 scATAC-pro installation</p>
      <ul id=""JCL3-16"" class=""wk-article__list wk-article__list--plain"">
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--plain"">- Compile from source code on GitHub.</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--plain"">- Run using a pre-configured Docker image.</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--plain"">- Install required dependencies (Python ≥3.7, R ≥4.0, Bowtie2, etc).</li>
      </ul>
      <p id=""JCL-P-42"">Execute the following command in your terminal to deploy scATAC-pro to the specified installation directory: YOUR_INSTALL_PATH/scATAC-pro_1.5.2</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-43"">>git clone <span><a href=""https://github.com/wbaopaul/scATAC-pro.git"" onclick=""javascript:window.open('https://github.com/wbaopaul/scATAC-pro.git');return false"">https://github.com/wbaopaul/scATAC-pro.git</a></span></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-44"">>cd scATAC-pro</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-45"">>make configure prefix=YOUR_INSTALL_PATH</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-46"">>make install</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-47"">2.2 Input requirements</p>
      <ul id=""JCL3-20"" class=""wk-article__list wk-article__list--bullet"">
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">FASTQ files for pair-end1 reads(pe1_fastq.gz), pair-end2 reads(pe2_fastq_gz) and cell barcords (index_fastq.gz)</li>
        <li class=""wk-article__list-item wk-article__list-item--bullet"">for data generated by 10x, you can just specify the path to each FASTQ file folder per sample</li>
      </ul>
      <p id=""JCL-P-50"">2.3 Step-by-step guide to running scATAC-pro</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-51"">Execute the scATAC-pro pipeline sequentially by configuring the PEAK_CALLER (eg, MACS2) and CELL_CALLER (eg, FILTER) parameters in the configure_user.txt file prior to runtime.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-52"">>scATAC-pro -s demplx_fastq</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-53"">-i pe1_fastq.gz,pe2_fastq.gz,index_fastq.gz</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-54"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-55""># or for 10x data</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-56"">>scATAC-pro -s demplx_fastq</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-57"">  -i pbmc_10x_fastqs/</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-58"">  -c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-59"">>scATAC-pro -s trimming</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-60"">-i output/demplxed_fastq/pbmc5k.demplxed.PE1.fastq.gz,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-61"">  output/demplxed_fastq/pbmc5k.demplxed.PE2.fastq.gz</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-62"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-63"">>scATAC-pro -s mapping</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-64"">-i output/trimmed_fastq/pbmc5k.trimmed.demplxed.PE1.fastq.gz,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-65"">  output/trimmed_fastq/pbmc5k.trimmed.demplxed.PE2.fastq.gz,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-66"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-67"">>scATAC-pro -s call_peak</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-68"">-i output/mapping_result/pbmc5k.positionsort.MAPQ30.bam</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-69"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-70"">>scATAC-pro -s aggr_signal</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-71"">-i output/mapping_result/pbmc5k.positionsort.MAPQ30.bam</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-72"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-73"">>scATAC-pro -s get_mtx -i output/summary/pbmc5k.fragments.tsv.gz,output/peaks/PEAK_CALLER/pbmc5k_features_BlacklistRemoved.bed</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-74"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-75"">>scATAC-pro -s qc_per_barcode -i output/summary/pbmc5k.fragments.tsv.gz,output/peaks/PEAK_CALLER/pbmc5k_features_BlacklistRemoved.bed</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-76"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-77"">>scATAC-pro -s call_cell</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-78"">-i output/raw_matrix/PEAK_CALLER/matrix.mtx</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-79"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-80"">>scATAC-pro -s get_bam4Cells</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-81"">-i output/mapping_result/pbmc5k.positionsort.bam,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-82"">output/filtered_matrix/PEAK_CALLER/CELL_CALLER/barcodes.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-83"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-84"">Some of the processing modules can be run together by a single command:</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-85"">In one mode, processing data including demplx_fastq, mapping, call_peak, get_mtx, aggr_signal, qc_per_barcode, call_cell, and get_bam4Cells.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-86"">>scATAC-pro -s process</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-87"">-i pe1.fastq.gz,pe2.fastq.gz,index.fastq.gz</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-88"">-c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-89""># or for 10x data</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-90"">>scATAC-pro -s process</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-91"">  -i PATH_TO_10x_fastqs_directory</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-92"">  -c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-93"">In another mode, conduct all processing modules except demultiplexing step.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-94"">>scATAC-pro -s process_no_dex</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-95"">  -i pe1_fastq,pe2_fastq</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-96"">  -c configure_user.txt</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-97""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 3: Analysis of single-cell chromatin accessibility data with ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-98"">The first thing we do is change to our desired working directory, set the number of threads we would like to use, and load our gene and genome annotations. Then, using ArchR, we import the fragment files from the output of Cell Ranger ATAC to create ArrowFiles and an ArchRProject.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-99"">3.1 Load ArchR</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-100"">>library(ArchR)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-101"">>library(parallel)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-102"">>library(ggplot2)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-103"">>inputFiles <- getTutorialData(“Hematopoiesis”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-104"">>set.seed(123)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-105"">>addArchRThreads(threads = 16)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-106""># We recommend setting threads to 1/2 to 3/4 of the total available cores.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-107"">>addArchRGenome(“hg38”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-108""># addArchRGenome(“hg19”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-109"">Note: ArchR has built-in support for “hg19,” “hg38,” “mm9,” and “mm10.” You can also use the createGeneAnnotation() and createGenomeAnnotation() functions to build your own genome and gene annotations.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-110"">3.2 Create ArrowFiles</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-111"">As a powerful tool for single-cell ATAC-seq data analysis, ArchR is compatible with diverse data input formats, with fragment and BAM files being the most commonly used. Subsequently, we employ the fragment files generated by the 10x Genomics Cell Ranger ATAC as input files in ArchR.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-112""># Locate Fragment Files</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-113"">>inputFiles <- c(“Sample1” = “/path/to/atac_pbmc_5k_analysis/outs/fragments.tsv.gz”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-114""># Create Arrow Files</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-115"">>ArrowFiles <- createArrowFiles(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-116""> inputFiles = inputFiles,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-117""> sampleNames = names(inputFiles),</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-118""> minTSS = 2,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-119""> # Dont set this too high because you can always increase later</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-120""> minFrags = 1000,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-121""> addTileMat = TRUE,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-122""> addGeneScoreMat = TRUE</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-123"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-124"">We can inspect the ArrowFiles object to see that it is actually just a character vector of Arrow file paths.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-125"">3.3 Per-cell quality control</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-126"">In ArchR, QC of scATAC-seq data is crucial for eliminating low-quality cells. This process focuses on 3 key aspects: the number of unique nuclear fragments, the signal-to-background ratio, and the fragment size distribution. In the prior step, we applied relaxed thresholds for the minimum transcription start site (minTSS) enrichment score and the minimum mapped ATAC-seq fragments per cell (minFrags). This allowed an initial evaluation of the data quality. For each sample, ArchR automatically generates a cell density heatmap of TSS enrichment score and number of ATAC-seq fragments. Arrow files creation produces a “QualityControl” folder in the current directory, containing 2 plots per sample. One plots log10(unique nuclear fragments) against TSS enrichment scores, with thresholds marked by dotted lines (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 2A</a></strong>). The other displays fragment size distributions (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 2B</a></strong>).</p><section class=""ejp-r-article-images""><figure class=""ejp-r-article-images__figure""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__image-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013')""><img class=""ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load"" src=""javascript:void(0);"" data-src=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F2.jpeg"" data-srcset=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F2.jpeg 2x"" srcset="""" alt=""F2""></a><figcaption class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013')"">Figure 2.: </a><div class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text"">Quality control and doublet detection of scATAC-seq data. (A–B) Quality control metrics of sample 1. (A) TSS enrichment score versus log<sub xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">10</sub>(unique nuclear fragments) per cell. Dotted lines represent filtering thresholds applied for downstream analysis. Cells passing these thresholds (n = 5278) exhibited a median of 14,877 fragments and a median TSS enrichment score of 20.64, indicating good data quality. Fragment size distribution (B) showing characteristic mono- and di-nucleosome peaks, supporting successful transposition and library construction. (C) Doublet identification plots. UMAP projection showing doublet enrichment scores (left), indicating the relative enrichment of simulated doublets compared to expectation. UMAP projection of doublet scores (middle), reflecting the statistical significance (−log<sub xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">10</sub> binomial-adjusted <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">p</em> value) of doublet enrichment for each cell. UMAP projection of simulated doublet density (right), visualizing the spatial distribution of synthetic doublets projected into the same low-dimensional embedding. These plots were generated during the addDoubletScores() step and are used to identify and filter potential doublets. LSI = latent semantic indexing, scATAC = single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, TSS = transcription start site, UMAP = Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection.</div></figcaption></figure></section><p id=""JCL-P-127"">3.4 Doublet Inference with ArchR</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-128"">Single-cell data from any platform is prone to doublets, where one droplet contains one barcoded bead and multiple nuclei. This makes reads from multiple cells appear as a single cell. It is especially problematic in developmental/trajectory data, as doublets can be mistaken for intermediate cell types or states. We can observe that the addition of doublet scores leads to the generation of 3 related plots: doublet enrichments (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 2C</a></strong>), doublet scores (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 2D</a></strong>), and doublet density (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F2', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 2E</a></strong>).</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-129"">> doubScores <- addDoubletScores(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-130"">input = ArrowFiles,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-131"">k = 10,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-132"">#Refers to how many cells near a “pseudo-doublet” to count.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-133"">knnMethod = “UMAP,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-134"">#Refers to the embedding to use for nearest neighbor search with doublet projection.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-135"">LSIMethod = 1</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-136"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-137"">3.5 Create an ArchRProject</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-138"">An ArchRProject serves as a centralized structure for integrating multiple Arrow files into a single, memory-efficient project. It enables rapid data access and manipulation, facilitating efficient interaction with Arrow files. As the foundation of most ArchR functions and analytical workflows, it streamlines data management and accelerates computational processes.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-139"">>archr_proj <- ArchRProject(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-140""> ArrowFiles = ArrowFiles,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-141""> outputDirectory = “ output_ArchR,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-142""> copyArrows = TRUE</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-143""> # It keeps an original Arrow file copy for later use, as we’ll modify them downstream.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-144"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-145"">>getAvailableMatrices(archr_proj)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-146"">Plotting sample fragment size distribution and TSS enrichment profiles.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-147""># Fragment size distributions</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-148"">>p1 <- plotFragmentSizes(ArchRProj = archr_proj)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-149""># TSS enrichment profiles</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-150"">>p2 <- plotTSSEnrichment(ArchRProj = archr_proj)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-151"">>plotPDF(p1,p2, name = “QC-Sample-FragSizes-TSSProfile.pdf,” ArchRProj = archr_proj, addDOC = FALSE, width = 5, height = 5)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-152"">We can save our archr_proj using saveArchRProject(), which will allow us to use this project in the future.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-153"">> # save this project</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-154"">>archr_proj <- saveArchRProject(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-155"">  ArchRProj = archr_proj,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-156"">  outputDirectory = “/Path_to_YourProject/archr_proj,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-157"">  load = TRUE</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-158"">  )</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-159""># load this project</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-160"">>archr_proj <- loadArchRProject(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-161"">path = “/Path_to_YourProject/archr_proj,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-162"">force = FALSE</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-163"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-164"">3.6 Filtering doublets from an ArchRProject</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-165"">A key part of this step is filterRatio, which is the maximum ratio of predicted doublets to filter, based on the number of pass—filter cells.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-166"">>archr_proj1 <- filterDoublets(archr_proj)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-167"">>archr_proj1 <- archr_proj1[which(archr_proj1$TSSEnrichment > 5 & archr_proj1$nFrags < 50000)]</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-168"">3.7 Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) of dimensionality reduction</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-169"">Dimensionality reduction in scATAC-seq is challenging due to the sparsity of the data, as most loci have zero accessible alleles, making traditional methods like PCA ineffective. To address this, latent semantic indexing (LSI),<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R23"">23</a></sup></sup><sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">,</sup><sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R24"">24</a></sup></sup> originally from natural language processing, is used. LSI normalizes data using term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and applies singular value decomposition (SVD) to reduce dimensionality while retaining important features. This transformation allows for effective visualization using UMAP or t-SNE, referred to as embeddings in ArchR.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-170"">>archr_proj1 <- addIterativeLSI(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-171"">ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-172"">useMatrix = “TileMatrix,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-173"">name = “IterativeLSI,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-174"">iterations = 2,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-175"">clusterParams = list(#See Seurat::FindClusters</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-176"">  resolution = c(0.2),</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-177"">  sampleCells = 5000,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-178"">  n.start = 10),</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-179"">varFeatures = 25000,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-180"">dimsToUse = 1:30</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-181"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-182"">3.8 Clustering with ArchR</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-183""># Clustering using Seurat’s `FindClusters()` function</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-184"">>archr_proj1 <- addClusters(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-185"">  input = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-186"">  reducedDims = “IterativeLSI”,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-187"">  method = “Seurat”,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-188"">  name = “Clusters”,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-189"">  resolution = 0.05</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-190"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-191"">3.9 Single-cell embeddings</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-192"">We use the addUMAP() function to run UMAP in ArchR and divide these cells into 5 clusters(<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 3A</a></strong>).</p><section class=""ejp-r-article-images""><figure class=""ejp-r-article-images__figure""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__image-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013')""><img class=""ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load"" src=""javascript:void(0);"" data-src=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F3.jpeg"" data-srcset=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F3.jpeg 2x"" srcset="""" alt=""F3""></a><figcaption class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013')"">Figure 3.: </a><div class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text"">Chromatin accessibility landscape and differential peak analysis across identified cell clusters. (A) UMAP embedding based on Iterative LSI showing 5 distinct clusters (C1–C5) identified from dataset. Each dot represents a single cell, colored by its cluster assignment. (B) Heatmap of top marker peaks across clusters (C1–C5), generated by markerHeatmap. Accessibility scores are <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Z</em> score normalized, highlighting cluster-specific chromatin signatures. Genomic coordinates of selected regions are shown on the y-axis. (C) MA plot (right) and volcano plot (left) of differentially accessible chromatin regions for cluster C4, generated using plotMarkers() from ArchR. Peaks were selected using thresholds of FDR ≤0.1 and log₂ fold change ≥1. Red points represent significantly upregulated peaks in C4 relative to other clusters. (D) Genome browser tracks showing chromatin accessibility at selected marker loci across 5 cell clusters (C1–C5). ATAC-seq signal tracks are grouped by clusters, with significantly upregulated peaks (FDR ≤0.1, Log₂FC ≥1) highlighted at each locus. ATAC = assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, FDR = false discovery rate, LSI = latent semantic indexing, MA = mean-average, UMAP = Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection.</div></figcaption></figure></section><p id=""JCL-P-193"">>archr_proj1 <- addUMAP(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-194""> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-195""> reducedDims = “IterativeLSI,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-196""> name = “UMAP,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-197""> nNeighbors = 30,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-198""> minDist = 0.5,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-199""> metric = “cosine”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-200"">>archr_proj1@embeddings</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-201"">>p3 <- plotEmbedding(archr_proj1, colorBy = “cellColData,” name = “Clusters,” embedding = “UMAP”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-202"">3.10 Batch effect correction with Harmony</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-203"">If there are subtle batch effects, you can add more LSI iterations and start with a lower initial clustering resolution. For strong batch effect differences, use ArchR’s Harmony tool for correction.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-204"">>archr_proj1 <- addHarmony(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-205""> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-206""> reducedDims = “IterativeLSI,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-207""> name = “Harmony,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-208""> groupBy = “Sample”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-209"">>archr_proj1 <- addClusters(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-210""> input = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-211""> reducedDims = “Harmony,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-212""> method = “Seurat,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-213""> name = “Harmony_Clusters,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-214""> maxClasters = 35,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-215""> resolution = 0.8)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-216"">>archr_proj1 <- addUMAP(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-217""> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-218""> reducedDims = “Harmony,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-219""> name = “UMAPHarmony,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-220""> nNeighbors = 30,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-221""> minDist = 0.5,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-222""> metric = “cosine”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-223"">Beyond our chosen approach, several popular batch correction and integration methods have been evaluated for scATAC-seq data, including LIGER,<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R25"">25</a></sup></sup> Harmony,<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R26"">26</a></sup></sup> RPCA,<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R27"">27</a></sup></sup> BBKNN,<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R28"">28</a></sup></sup> and scVI.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R29"">29</a></sup></sup> These tools differ in their underlying assumptions and performance across various feature spaces such as peaks, genomic windows, or gene activity matrices. Notably, only a minority (~27%) of integration attempts across diverse mouse brain datasets yielded improvements over unintegrated data, emphasizing the importance of feature selection.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R30"">30</a></sup></sup> LIGER showed robust batch correction across peak and window spaces, though sometimes introduced artificial substructures. Harmony retained more biological variation but exhibited occasional subtype overlaps. RPCA and BBKNN offered a balance between correction and signal retention in small-scale datasets, though with limited scalability.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-224"">Overall, when integrating scATAC-seq datasets, careful selection of feature space and tool is essential, as current methods often struggle to simultaneously remove batch effects and preserve biological fidelity—particularly in high-dimensional contexts.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-225"">3.11 Defining cluster identity</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-226"">Through manual annotation, we defined the 5 clusters as 4 cell types.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-227"">>markersGS <- getMarkerFeatures(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-228""> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-229""> useMatrix = “GeneScoreMatrix,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-230""> groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-231""> bias = c(“TSSEnrichment,” “log10(nFrags)”),</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-232""> testMethod = “wilcoxon”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-233"">>markerList <- getMarkers(markersGS, cutOff = “FDR≤0.05 & Log2FC≥1.0”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-234"">>markerGenes <- c(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-235""> “CD34,” #Early Progenitor</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-236""> ”GATA1,” #Erythroid</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-237""> ”CD79A,” “MS4A1,” “CD19,” #B-Cells</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-238""> “CD14,” “MPO,” #Monocytes</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-239""> ”CD3D,” “CD8A,”#TCells</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-240""> ”NCAM1” #NK)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-241"">>p4 <- plotEmbedding(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-242""> ArchRProj = archr_proj1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-243""> colorBy = “GeneScoreMatrix,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-244""> name = markerGenes,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-245""> embedding = “UMAP,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-246""> quantCut = c(0.01, 0.95),</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-247""> imputeWeights = NULL)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-248"">>cluster_annotations <- c(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-249""> “C1” = “Monocyte,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-250""> ”C2” = “Monocyte,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-251""> “C3” = “B Cell,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-252""> ”C4” = “T Cell,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-253""> “C5” = “NK Cell”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-254"">>current_clusters <- archr_proj1$Clusters</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-255"">>archr_proj1$celltype <- cluster_annotations[as.character(current_clusters)]</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-256"">>p5 <- plotEmbedding(archr_proj1, colorBy = “cellColData,” name = “celltype,” embedding = “UMAP”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-257""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 4: Calling peaks with ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-258"">Before calling peaks in ArchR, you must first run addGroupCoverages(), as ArchR relies on these group coverage objects for peak calling.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-259""># Making Pseudo-bulk Replicates</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-260"">> archr_proj <- addGroupCoverages(ArchRProj = archr_proj1, groupBy = “Clusters”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-261"">Peak calling was performed using MACS2 via ArchR’s “addReproduciblePeakSet()” function, with the parameters “--nomodel --shift -100 --extsize 200 --qvalue 0.05.” This configuration is recommended for scATAC-seq data, as it accounts for Tn5 transposase insertion sites and avoids model mis-specification in sparse single-cell data. Although ArchR includes a built-in peak caller, MACS2 is preferred due to its improved sensitivity and reproducibility.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-262"">To ensure the robustness of peak calling, we evaluated 3 representative MACS2 parameter sets that varied in “—qvalue” and “—extsize.” All configurations yielded the same number of final union peaks (65,015) after ArchR’s reproducibility filtering, with only 8 peaks overlapping ENCODE blacklist regions in each case (<0.01%). These results indicate that peak detection in our dataset is highly stable and minimally affected by small changes in parameterization.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-263"">For successful integration of MACS2, ArchR locates the executable through the system PATH or pip installation. If not automatically detected, the user can specify the exact binary location via the “pathToMacs2” argument. We recommend verifying the MACS2 version being used to avoid conflicts in multi-environment setups.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-264""># pathToMacs2 <- findMacs2()</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-265"">>pathToMacs2 <- normalizePath(“/usr/local/bin/macs2”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-266"">>archr_proj2 <- addReproduciblePeakSet(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-267""> ArchRProj = archr_proj2,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-268""> groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-269""> pathToMacs2 = pathToMacs2,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-270""> peakMethod = “MACS2,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-271""> additionalParams = “--nomodel --shift -100 --extsize 200 --qvalue 0.05”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-272"">>getPeakSet(archr_proj2)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-273""># Adding a Peak Matrix</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-274"">>archr_proj3 <- addPeakMatrix(archr_proj2)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-275""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 5: Differential chromatin accessibility peaks analysis</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-276"">In many cases, identifying peaks that are unique to a specific cluster or a small group of clusters is crucial. In ArchR, this can be achieved in an unsupervised manner by utilizing the addMarkerFeatures() function in combination with the useMatrix = “PeakMatrix” parameter. This approach allows for the detection of cluster-specific chromatin accessibility features, providing valuable insights into the distinct regulatory landscapes of individual clusters.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-277"">>markersPeaks <- getMarkerFeatures(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-278""> ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-279""> useMatrix = “PeakMatrix,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-280""> groupBy = “Clusters,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-281""> bias = c(“TSSEnrichment,” “log10(nFrags)”),</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-284"">ArchR provides multiple plotting functions that interface with objects returned by SummarizedExperiment, enabling visualization of marker peaks within the ArchR framework(<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F3', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 3B–D</a></strong>).</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-306""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 6: Motif and feature enrichment analysis with ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-307"">After identifying marker peaks, we can perform motif enrichment analysis on these peaks using the peakAnnoEnrichment() function. Marker peaks are typically derived from significantly differentially accessible peaks, identified through the getMarkerFeatures() function in ArchR. By using peakAnnoEnrichment(), we test whether these peaks are enriched for specific transcription factor (TF) binding motifs, helping to uncover potential TF regulatory relationships(<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 4A</a></strong>). This step provides critical insights into the gene regulatory mechanisms within different cell populations.</p><section class=""ejp-r-article-images""><figure class=""ejp-r-article-images__figure""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__image-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013')""><img class=""ejp-r-article-images__img js-lazy-load lazy-load"" src=""javascript:void(0);"" data-src=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview.02118581-202603000-00013.F4.jpeg"" data-srcset=""https://images.journals.lww.com/bls/ArticleViewerPreview@2.02118581-202603000-00013.F4.jpeg 2x"" srcset="""" alt=""F4""></a><figcaption class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-link"" onclick=""showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013')"">Figure 4.: </a><div class=""ejp-r-article-images__figcaption-text"">TF motif enrichment and footprinting analysis across scATAC-seq-defined clusters. (A) Heatmap showing TF motif enrichment in differentially accessible peaks across cell clusters. Motifs from the CIS-BP database were annotated via addMotifAnnotations(), and significance is represented as normalized enrichment scores (color gradient) and adjusted <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">p</em> values (−log10[p adj]). Each row represents a transcription factor motif and each column a cell cluster. (B) Rank-sorted motif variability plot showing TF motifs with the highest variability across 5 cell clusters (C1–C5). Each dot represents a TF motif, ranked by variability on the y-axis, which is calculated as the standard deviation of <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">z</em> scores across all cells. Variability reflects cell-to-cell heterogeneity in motif accessibility. Highly variable motifs are labeled and represent potential regulators of cell type-specific chromatin landscapes. (C) ChromVAR deviation score distributions for selected TF motifs across 5 cell clusters. The ridge plot shows smoothed deviation <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">z</em> scores for 7 immune-related TF motifs across clusters. Higher scores indicate greater motif accessibility. Imputation was applied to account for data sparsity in scATAC-seq. (D) TF footprinting using ArchR with Tn5 bias subtraction. Footprinting analysis was performed on selected TF motifs (PAX5_709, CEBPA_155, TCF7L2_762, and EOMES_788) using pseudo-bulk chromatin accessibility data grouped by clusters. scATAC = single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, TF = transcription factor.</div></figcaption></figure></section><p id=""JCL-P-308"">> archr_proj3 <- addMotifAnnotations(ArchRProj = archr_proj3, motifSet = “cisbp,” name = “Motif”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-309""># Motif Enrichment in Marker Peaks</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-310"">>enrichMotifs <- peakAnnoEnrichment(</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-313"">  peakAnnotation = “Motif,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-314"">  cutOff = “FDR≤0.1 & Log2FC≥0.5”)</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-317""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 7: ChromVAR deviations enrichment</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-318"">ChromVAR is an R package designed to analyze sparse single-cell ATAC-seq data by quantifying variability in chromatin accessibility across peaks sharing the same motif or annotation while correcting for technical biases.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R20"">20</a></sup></sup> In ArchR, this is achieved by first using chromVAR::getBackgroundPeaks() to define a set of matched background peaks, and then applying the addDeviationsMatrix() function to compute motif deviation scores for each cell across all annotated motifs. We can plot variable deviations (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 4B</a></strong>). This process generates a “MotifMatrix” that captures chromatin accessibility variation associated with TF binding. Through the names of the features we are interested in, we have plotted the distribution of chromVAR deviation scores for each cluster (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 4C</a></strong>).</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-319"">> if(“Motif” %ni% names(archr_proj3@peakAnnotation)){</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-320"">archr_proj3 <- addMotifAnnotations(ArchRProj = archr_proj3, motifSet = “cisbp,” name = “Motif”)}</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-321"">>archr_proj3 <- addBgdPeaks(archr_proj3)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-322"">>archr_proj3 <- addDeviationsMatrix(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-323"">  ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-324"">  peakAnnotation = “Motif,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-325"">  force = TRUE)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-326"">>plotVarDev <- getVarDeviations(archr_proj3, name = “MotifMatrix,” plot = TRUE)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-327""># extract a subset of motifs for downstream analysis</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-328"">>motifs <- c(“GATA1,” “CEBPA,” “EBF1,” “IRF4,” “TBX21,” “PAX5,” “Eomes,” “Nfil3”,”LEF1,” “TCF7”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-329"">>markerMotifs <- getFeatures(archr_proj3, select = paste(motifs, collapse=”|”), useMatrix = “MotifMatrix”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-330"">>markerMotifs <- grep(“z:,” markerMotifs, value = TRUE)</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-332"">>plotGroups(ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-337"">We can visualize the distribution of chromVAR deviation scores across each cluster and overlay the corresponding TF <em xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">z</em> scores onto the UMAP embedding. Additionally, gene scores for these TF can also be overlaid on the UMAP to provide a comprehensive view of their activity patterns across different cell populations.</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-340"">  ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-348"">>plotEmbedding(</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-354""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 8: TF motif annotation and footprinting analysis in ArchR</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-355"">TF footprinting analysis predicts the precise binding sites of TFs on the chromatin, which typically requires high sequencing depth to achieve accurate results. To address this limitation, an integrative analytical strategy is implemented by systematically correlating predicted TF binding sites with the spatial distribution patterns of Tn5 transposase insertion sites. The accuracy of this footprinting analysis heavily depends on the availability of a reliable list of predicted binding sites for the TF of interest.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-356"">Motif annotation in the ArchR workflow is performed using the addMotifAnnotations() function, which applies sequence matching algorithms to scan chromatin-accessible regions (peaks) for DNA sequences matching the target TF motifs. The results are stored in the ArchRProject object as binary annotations (0 = motif absent, 1 = motif present), indicating the presence or absence of the motif in each peak. While this approach efficiently identifies canonical motif elements, its accuracy can be limited by motif degeneracy, potentially overlooking non-canonical or low-affinity binding sites.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-357"">Once motif annotations are generated, TF footprinting analysis is conducted using the getFootprints() function, which requires 2 inputs: the ArchRProject object and a set of motif coordinates in GenomicRanges format, derived from the getPositions() function. This procedure quantifies protection patterns at predicted TF binding sites, inferred from transposase (Tn5) insertion profiles, thus enabling the detection of TF occupancy at single-base resolution.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-358"">This analysis framework is part of the validated ArchR pipeline, which provides scalable and efficient single-cell chromatin accessibility analysis, particularly suited for high-throughput scATAC-seq datasets.<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R11"">11</a></sup></sup> The binary motif annotation structure, compatible with BSgenome, ensures computational efficiency for large-scale datasets and delivers structured inputs for downstream inference of GRNs.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-359"">>motifPositions <- getPositions(archr_proj3)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-360"">>motifs <- c(“GATA1,” “CEBPA,” “EBF1,” “IRF4,” “TBX21,” “PAX5”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-361"">>markerMotifs <- unlist(lapply(motifs, function(x) grep(x, names(motifPositions), value = TRUE)))</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-362"">>markerMotifs <- markerMotifs[markerMotifs %ni% “SREBF1_22”]</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-363"">>if(is.null(archr_proj3@projectMetadata$GroupCoverages$Clusters)){archr_proj3 <- addGroupCoverages(ArchRProj = archr_proj3, groupBy = “Clusters”)}</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-364"">>seFoot <- getFootprints(ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-365""> positions = motifPositions[markerMotifs],</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-366""> groupBy = “Clusters”)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-367"">The resulting footprints can be visualized using the plotFootprints() function, which displays the distribution of motif insertions, reflecting the binding activity of the TFs.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-368"">To eliminate technical noise and reduce false-positive signals introduced by the sequence preference of Tn5 transposase, normalization for Tn5 bias is essential in footprinting analysis. This correction improves the specificity of footprint detection and ensures the reliability of downstream analyses. In this study, we applied 2 normalization strategies implemented in ArchR: subtracting Tn5 (<strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><a href=""javascript:void(0)"" onclick=""javascript:showSlideShowByImageID('F4', '02118581-202603000-00013');"">Fig. 4D</a></strong>) bias and dividing by Tn5 bias, each providing a distinct approach to account for bias-related artifacts in Tn5 insertion patterns.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-369""># Subtracting the Tn5 Bias</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-370"">>plotFootprints(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-371"">  seFoot = seFoot,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-372"">  ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-373"">  normMethod = “Subtract,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-374"">  plotName = “Footprints-Subtract-Bias,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-375"">  addDOC = FALSE,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-376"">  smoothWindow = 5)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-377""># Dividing by the Tn5 Bias</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-378"">>plotFootprints(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-379"">  seFoot = seFoot,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-380"">  ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-381"">  normMethod = “Divide,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-382"">  plotName = “Footprints-Divide-Bias,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-383"">  addDOC = FALSE,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-384"">  smoothWindow = 5)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-385""># Footprinting Without Normalization for Tn5 Bias</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-386"">>plotFootprints(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-387"">  seFoot = seFoot,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-388"">  ArchRProj = archr_proj3,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-389"">  normMethod = “None,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-390"">  plotName = “Footprints-No-Normalization,”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-391"">  addDOC = FALSE,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-392"">  smoothWindow = 5)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-393""><strong xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0"">Step 9: Transcriptional regulatory network construction with SCENIC+</strong></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-394"">Here, we employ SCENIC+, a comprehensive framework that integrates single-cell chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and TF motif information to reconstruct enhancer-driven gene regulatory networks (eGRNs).<sup xmlns:mrws=""http://webservices.ovid.com/mrws/1.0""><sup><a class=""ejp-citation-link js-ejp-citation-link"" data-reference-links=""R21"">21</a></sup></sup></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-395"">The resulting network allows high-resolution exploration of transcriptional regulation.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-396"">While early steps of the chromatin accessibility analysis (eg, peak calling, clustering, and motif enrichment) were performed on an ATAC-only dataset, SCENIC+ analysis was conducted using a paired single-cell multiome dataset (RNA + ATAC) from 10x Genomics. This ensured compatibility with SCENIC+’s multi-modal regulatory network reconstruction framework.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-397"">9.1 Install SCENIC+ and Dependencies</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-398"">Installing SCENIC+ in the new conda environment is highly recommended. It can be installed in a conda environment as follows:</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-399"">>conda create --name scenicplus python=3.11 -y</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-400"">>conda activate scenicplus</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-401"">>git clone <span><a href=""https://github.com/aertslab/scenicplus"" onclick=""javascript:window.open('https://github.com/aertslab/scenicplus');return false"">https://github.com/aertslab/scenicplus</a></span></p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-402"">>cd scenicplus</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-403"">>pip install.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-404"">9.2 Preprocess scATAC-seq Data using pycisTopic</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-405"">SCENIC+ enables the integration of ArchR-filtered fragment count matrices and cell metadata into a cisTopic object, facilitating subsequent topic modeling and GRN inference. Additionally, predefined region sets can be used to bypass topic modeling, though this may limit the resolution of regulatory pattern discovery. The flexibility in input formats facilitates integration with existing analysis pipelines.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-406"">We begin by creating a cisTopic object, then add metadata to the cisTopic object, and subsequently infer doublets from the scATAC-seq data.</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-407"">>from pycisTopic.cistopic_class import create_cistopic_object_from_fragments</p>

      <p id=""JCL-P-413"">{sample_id}.fragments_stats_per_cb.parquet’</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-414"">)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-415"">  ).to_pandas().set_index(“</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-416"">CB”</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-417"">).loc[sample_id_to_barcodes_passing_filters[sample_id]]</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-418"">  cistopic_obj = create_cistopic_object_from_fragments(</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-419"">  path_to_fragments = fragments_dict[sample_id],</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-420"">  path_to_regions = path_to_regions,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-421"">  path_to_blacklist = path_to_blacklist,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-422"">  metrics = sample_metrics,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-423"">  valid_bc = sample_id_to_barcodes_passing_filters[sample_id],</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-424"">  n_cpu = 1,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-425"">  project = sample_id,</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-426"">  split_pattern = ‘-’)</p>
      <p id=""JCL-P-427"">>cistopic_obj_list.append(cistopic_obj)</p>

            __doPostBack('hypSubscribeToAlerts');

    function alerts_ShowSubscribeeTOCPopup(journalTitle, journalId, subscriptionType, displaySubscriptionType) {
        $('#' + 'ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscriptionType').val(subscriptionType);
        var subscribeToEtocPopup = $find('subscribeToEtoc');
        subscribeToEtocPopup.show();
        document.getElementsByTagName( 'html' )[0].classList.add('no-scroll');
        var modelPopupState = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenSubscribeToEtocPopupState');
        var emailTextBox = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_txtEmailAddress');
        var thanksPanel = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_pnlAuthenticatedUser');
        var mainPanel = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_pnlMain');
        var thankYouMessageUnAuthenticated = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_lblThankYouMessage');
        var thankYouMessageAuthenticated = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_lblAuthenticatedUserTitle');

        if (!displaySubscriptionType) {
            displaySubscriptionType = subscriptionType;
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showthanksmessage') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = ""block"";
            mainPanel.style.display = ""none"";
            thankYouMessageAuthenticated.innerHTML = ""Thank you for subscribing to the "" + displaySubscriptionType + "" for "" + journalTitle + ""."";
        }

        if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail') {
            thanksPanel.style.display = ""none"";
            mainPanel.style.display = ""block"";

            thankYouMessageUnAuthenticated.innerHTML = ""Thank you for choosing to subscribe to the "" + displaySubscriptionType + "" for "" + journalTitle + ""."";
        }

        if ($('.etoc-popup') != null) {
            document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenJournalId').value = journalId;

            if (modelPopupState.value == 'showemail')
                emailTextBox.focus();
        }
    }

    $('.js-close').on('click', function () {
        document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_txtEmailAddress').value = """";
        document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_cvEmailError').style.display = ""none"";
        var pageUrl = document.getElementById('ctl00_ctl51_Header_UserActionTools_SubscribeToEtocPopupControl_hiddenConfirmSubscriptionPageUrl');
        var subscribeeTocPopup = $find('subscribeToEtoc');
        if (subscribeeTocPopup != null) {
            subscribeeTocPopup.hide();
            document.getElementsByTagName( 'html' )[0].classList.remove('no-scroll');
            if (pageUrl.value !== '' && pageUrl.value !== window.location.pathname)
                window.location = pageUrl.value;
        }
        return false;
    });
</script>

Pretrained and fi netuned models exhibited nearly identical hierarchical block structures across all tasks. Early layers showed low prediction correlations with later layers while predictions within each block were highly correlated ( r > .95 among layers 5-12) The transition point around layer 4 corresponds precisely to where probe accuracy plateaus, suggesting that layers 14 progressively build task-relevant representations, while layers 5-12 maintain these compressed representations with minimal additional transformation. #### SAE features are enriched for REs

After pretraining the 0.5-weighted Nucleotide GPT, we trained an SAE on the intermediate activations of the model's residual stream. The SAE expanded the 2048-dimensional activations to a sparse 8192-dimensional latent space and then reconstructed the original representation. Linear probes trained on these sparse SAE features achieved compar able performance to probes trained on dense activations across classification tasks (Supplementary Table 1), suggesting that sparse decomposition may preserve task-relevant information. By extracting the top sequences that maximally activated each latent feature, we manually annotated f eatures using RE alignment tool Dfam [24]. REs are DNA sequences present in multiple copies that constitute 30-60% of mammalian genomes. Transposable elements (TEs), a major class of REs, are mobile DNA sequences that propagate within genomes [25]. While they can threaten genomic integrity if not properly regulated and may have deleterious effects, they can also represent a significant source of genetic variation that has contributed to evolutionary innovation [26].

Several SAE features were notably enriched for TEs. Two latent features consistently responded to sequences with high similarity to the THE1D and THE1B repeats -elements belonging to the endogenous retrovirus-like mammalian-apparent long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposon (ERVL-MaLR) class (Table 6) [27]. Additional features highlighted distinct regions of Long Interspersed Nuclear Element (LINE) retrotransposons. One mapped primarily to the 3 ′ untranslated regions, which contain conserved polyadenylation signals and RNA motifs, while another concentrated on 5 ′ regions that harbor internal promoters for certain L1PA subfamilies (Table 6) [28]. Features also showed strong activation on sequences aligning to subfamilies of the highly abundant Alu family of Short Interspersed Nuclear Elements (SINEs) (Table 6). Alu elements are mobile DNA sequences comprising over 10% of the human genome and have been found to contribute significantly to genomic evolution through RNA editing, exonization, and transcript variation [29].

#### REs show distinct enrichment patterns in regulatory r egions

To understand how REs are distributed across functional genomic regions, we performed enrichment analysis using the Genomic Association Tester (GAT) comparing 46 RE classes against promoters,

Traditional Cell Type Annotation.
First, we compared the performance of scCLIP-GPT and OKR-CELL trained on noisy data in traditional cell annotation tasks, and we also included the results of models trained on original data for comparison. As shown in the Figure 4B, the performance of scCLIP-GPT trained on noisy data degrades on most datasets, with the F1-score dropping by 6% (from 73.3 to 68.9) on the spleen dataset; in contrast, our OKR-CELL shows no significant performance decline across all datasets and outperforms the former significantly. For example, on the colon dataset, the F1-score of OKR-CELL(noisy) is 15.7% higher than that of scCLIP-GPT(noisy), which is notably larger than the gap between the two under non-noisy conditions. Surprisingly, OKR-CELL(noisy) trained on fabricated data even achieves performance improvements on some datasets. For instance, the F1-score for classification on the colon dataset increases by 5.5% (from 67.0 to 70.7), and the accuracy on the spleen dataset rises by 5.5% (from 77.6 to 78.8). We analyze the potential reasons for this result as follows: 1) The cell encoder is not very sensitive to the expression values of input transcriptome genes, and the noise injection method through expression value perturbation actually enhances the robustness of the cell encoder; 2) The cell types in the colon dataset have a large number of similar or identical cell samples in the original training set, which helps the model learn strong discriminative capabilities for such cells from noisy data. Overall, our OKR-CELL model exhibits excellent robustness to noisy training data, which enables it to achieve better performance in more extreme data scenarios.",
